articles.title: 'Screamed, threatened employees': Nvidia ex-HR's allegations against Jensen Huang resurface
articles.summary: Allegations dating back nearly two decades that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang verbally abused employees, threatened them and made sexually explicit
articles.body: Allegations dating back nearly two decades that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang verbally abused employees, threatened them and made sexually explicit remarks have resurfaced amid questions over his tenure as the CEO of the semiconductor giant, according to a report by Bloomberg citing court documents from a 2007 lawsuit.The allegations were made by two former Nvidia employees, Stephen Pettigrew, the company's first in-house lawyer, and Michael Winston, who served as senior vice president for human resources. Both alleged that they faced retaliation after raising concerns about Huang's treatment of employees.Pettigrew, who joined Nvidia in September 1999 and was dismissed in June 2006, alleged that he was fired after flagging the conduct of company executives. Nvidia, however, attributed his termination to performance-related issues, according to court filings in California.In a brief filed by Pettigrew's lawyers in a lawsuit alleging age discrimination and wrongful termination, he claimed Huang regularly intimidated and verbally abused employees."He would scream at them, threaten them with extreme bodily harm and make sexually oriented comments while thrusting his hips in a demonstration of the sex act," the filing stated.Pettigrew also cited instances in which an unnamed senior Nvidia executive allegedly threatened an employee and made sexually explicit remarks. The lawsuit sought more than $2.6 million in damages. Nvidia filed counterclaims seeking the return of corporate documents. The dispute was resolved through a confidential settlement in December 2009.Also Read| Beyond Nvidia: Inside 7 decades of the US-China spy warAnother employee alleged retaliationWinston, Nvidia's former senior vice president for human resources, filed a discrimination complaint in 2005 alleging that he was dismissed after objecting to "Huang's abusive treatment of employees, including conduct he believed constituted sexual harassment," according to court documents cited in Pettigrew's case.Winston joined Nvidia in September 2004 but spent only four weeks at the company, according to depositions cited in the court filings.Nvidia subsequently reached a confidential settlement with Winston for more than $1 million, according to The New York Times, which had previously reported details of the complaints.Winston later became known for his efforts to expose alleged corporate wrongdoing. A jury awarded him $3.8 million in damages after he claimed Countrywide Financial Corp. had fired him for raising concerns about its lending practices. However, a federal appeals court overturned the award.Both Pettigrew and Winston are now dead. Attorneys who represented them, as well as their family members, could not be reached for comment, according to Bloomberg.Huang's leadership style under scrutinyThe allegations have resurfaced as Huang faces questions over his leadership and the possibility of returning to the position he held for more than three decades. He resigned earlier this month following disclosures about multiple alleged affairs, including one involving a direct report and another involving a suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with Huang is being investigated by the US Justice Department, according to the report.Huang has previously acknowledged putting intense pressure on employees, saying he was "torturing" those working closely with him to ensure they delivered their best work. Reports have also described instances in which he allegedly demeaned subordinates during his long tenure at the company.A representative for Huang rejected the allegations, saying, "These false allegations are from over 20 years ago and were made by two fired employees. The thousands of employees who have shown support for Jensen over the last week show they are false."Nvidia representatives did not respond to requests for comment, Bloomberg reported.At 63, Huang has described his demanding management approach as a response to the pressures of operating in a rapidly changing technology industry. He has often spoken about the need for urgency and moving quickly, while also expressing pride in not laying off employees and regret over the one occasion when he did so.Some of Huang's allies in Silicon Valley and Nvidia employees have reportedly backed efforts for his reinstatement. However, the company's board and senior management have publicly rejected the prospect of his return so far.Despite accounts of his demanding management style, Huang is often described as congenial and lighthearted during public appearances and events outside Nvidia. Employees who reported to him have also maintained a respectful tone when discussing him, even while acknowledging that he could be intimidating.The allegations against Huang date back to his early years at Nvidia, which went public in 1999. Pettigrew, a former electrical design engineer who had previously worked at three major law firms, was hired in September that year and remained with the company until his dismissal in June 2006.The claims in the two employees' complaints were allegations made in legal proceedings and were not established as findings of a court.You use AI every day. articles.title: Florida battles historic flooding as storms move further north
articles.summary: Water levels across central Florida continued to rise on Friday even as rainfall eased, prompting authorities to warn residents in flood-prone areas along
articles.body: Water levels across central Florida continued to rise on Friday even as rainfall eased, prompting authorities to warn residents in flood-prone areas along the state's longest river to prepare for possible evacuations.The city of Rockledge urged people living in its low-lying western neighbourhoods to be ready to leave their homes while conditions remained safe.Thousands of residents could be affected as days of heavy rainfall flow into the St. Johns River and its surrounding lakes, according to meteorologists from the National Weather Service in Melbourne."We're so concerned with the Saint Johns River," said Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist in Melbourne. He warned that the large volume of water would cause the river to keep rising over the coming days.Near Cocoa, the river crossed its previous record level set in 1953 on Thursday. The National Weather Service forecast that flooding would continue until early next week.Heavy rainfall has already inundated large parts of Florida's Atlantic coast, leaving some residents stranded in floodwaters in the northeastern region of the state.Flood warnings and watches issued by the National Weather Service cover an area stretching nearly 200 miles (320 kilometres), from south of Melbourne to Jacksonville. Forecasters expected another 6 inches (15 centimetres) of rain in some areas through Saturday, while isolated locations could receive as much as 12 inches (30 centimetres).Hundreds of emergency personnel were deployed along the coast to assist affected communities.In the Florida Shores neighbourhood of Edgewater, police officers waded through knee-deep water on Friday to pull residents to safety using a small boat. Further south in Brevard County, rescue teams used airboats to navigate flooded roads and reach stranded people. Authorities had carried out nearly 100 high-water rescues in the area a day earlier.Some parts of Florida's east coast have received more than 17 inches (43 centimetres) of rain since Tuesday, according to preliminary National Weather Service figures. The state had also experienced heavy rainfall earlier this month, with several locations already recording their wettest November on record.* Flooding disrupts Thanksgiving preparationsThe severe flooding has also disrupted holiday plans for residents preparing for Thanksgiving.Sara Hernandez had decorated her home and purchased groceries for the holiday before floodwaters reached her front and back doors on Thursday morning. By Friday, several inches of water had entered her house.She said she was uncertain about how she and her family would manage the situation."I have never ever seen this much water in the 25 years I've been in Florida," Hernandez said in a message. "It's never flooded here."Hernandez, who runs a cleaning business, said removing the water would be difficult and she could not afford to replace damaged household appliances. She had hoped to make the holiday special for her four children."At least we are safe and dry," she said while staying at her brother-in-law's house.Meanwhile, rain could affect much of the US Eastern Seaboard during the holiday week, as millions of Americans prepare to travel.The low-pressure system responsible for Florida's heavy rainfall was expected to move northeast over the weekend, bringing rain to the coastal areas of Georgia and the Carolinas, said Scott Kleebauer, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service's Weather Prediction Center in Maryland.Another weather system moving in from the Atlantic could bring further rainfall from the mid-Atlantic region to New England on Sunday and Monday.Forecasters said the system could develop into a subtropical or tropical storm, bringing strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding to the southeastern and mid-Atlantic regions through early next week.Meteorologists are also monitoring the possibility of a third coastal system developing around the middle of next week and moving from the Southeast towards New England.Kleebauer said the third system could be stronger and potentially affect several areas on Wednesday and Thanksgiving Day.* Flood risk could continue into 2027The storms affecting Florida this week have been driven by persistent high pressure over Virginia, along with a low-pressure system and a stationary front in the Gulf. Together, these weather conditions have pushed a continuous flow of moisture from the ocean across the Florida Peninsula.The weather pattern is also linked to El Niño, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean near the equator that influences weather conditions across the world. Florida's dry season generally lasts from October to May.However, the slow-moving St. Johns River poses a prolonged flooding threat to communities along its banks. Forecasters expect El Niño conditions to continue through the spring.Ulrich said the heavy rainfall had left the soil saturated even before the beginning of Florida's usual dry season. He warned that flooding along the river could continue well into the new year and possibly through 2027.Meanwhile, heavy rainfall also caused widespread flooding across parts of California, including areas between Los Angeles and San Francisco. Several neighbourhoods were inundated, forcing motorists to abandon vehicles stranded in floodwaters. A long section of coastal Highway 1 was also closed because of rockfalls and mudslides.Two people, a man and a woman, were found dead in Chino on Friday following the heavy rainfall, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department.The woman had been swept downstream after rescue teams failed to save her from the water a day earlier. The man's body was discovered during the search for her. Authorities had not immediately released further details about the man.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: A single mother of five from Ballajura, Australia, is preparing to buy her dream home after winning $300,000 on a scratch card.
articles.body: A single mother of five from Ballajura, Australia, is preparing to buy her dream home after winning $300,000 on a scratch card. The woman, who is in her 50s and also has four grandchildren, spent 16 years living in Homeswest public housing while raising her children and continuing her education. She said the unexpected jackpot would allow her to put a deposit on a semi-rural property, pay off her HECS debt and create more space for her growing family. The winner discovered the prize while playing her usual midweek scratch card during a coffee break.How the mother of five from Ballajura discovered a $300,000 scratch card jackpot during her coffee breakThe winner discovered the prize through a routine she followed every Wednesday. She regularly bought scratch cards and played them during her coffee break. On this occasion, she was close to finishing the ticket when she initially thought she had won $15,000. After checking it again, she realised the prize was actually $300,000.She immediately called her daughters, and they went together to Ballajura News, where she regularly purchased her tickets, to celebrate with the shop's staff. The mother told PerthNow that she enjoyed seeing their reactions when she revealed the jackpot.Rather than using the money for a luxury purchase, she plans to put it towards a home that can accommodate her extended family and provide greater financial security. The semi-rural property she has long hoped to own is now within reach, with the winnings also allowing her to address her outstanding HECS debt.Ballajura mother of five spent 16 years raising her children in public housingThe woman spent 16 years in Homeswest housing, raising her five children while also educating herself. Now in her 50s, she has established and runs a not-for-profit organisation, drawing on her own experiences to help others who need support. She also works alongside two of her daughters.Speaking to PerthNow, the mother said she understood how important it was to receive the right help during difficult circumstances. Her family has since grown to include four grandchildren, and she hopes her lottery win will allow them to have more room together.She said she had always wanted to move to a semi-rural property and intended to use the $300,000 prize towards a deposit while also clearing her HECS debt. articles.title: In 2002, Kentucky researchers examined 20 treated subgrade sections across 14 road sites; after 8–15 years, treated soil’s CBR ranged from 24 to 59, versus 2 for untreated soil
articles.summary: A groundbreaking study from the University of Kentucky reveals that chemical treatments significantly improve road subgrade strength, ensuring long-lasting pavement performance. Discover the key findings and implications for transportation infrastructure.
articles.body: Roads depend on the soil beneath them to support traffic and prevent pavement damage. When the underlying layer is weak, repeated vehicle loads can contribute to cracking, rutting and surface deterioration. In a 2002 study, researchers at the University of Kentucky examined whether chemical treatments could improve road subgrade strength over the long term. They studied 20 treated sections across 14 sites where the pavements had already been in service for approximately 8 to 15 years. The findings appeared in Long-Term Benefits of Stabilizing Soil Subgrades, published in June 2002 by the Kentucky Transportation Center. Tommy C. Hopkins, Tony L. Beckham, Liecheng Sun, Bixian Ni and Barry Butcher conducted the research. The full report is available through the University of Kentucky’s UKnowledge repository.Researchers examined 20 treated road sectionsChemical stabilisation of road subgrades had been used in Kentucky since the mid-1980s to improve foundation strength. The study aimed to find out whether these improvements had lasted after years of traffic and weathering. The researchers studied 20 chemically treated sections at 14 road sites. Scientists took approximately 455 samples of soil cores from both treated soil and non-treated soil beneath it. In the experiments, scientists used several types of chemical stabiliser: hydrated lime, Portland cement, a combination of hydrated lime and Portland cement and a by-product of hydrated lime production known in the study as MKD.Treated soil recorded a much higher CBR valueOne of the tests measured the California Bearing Ratio (CBR), which compares the penetration resistance of the soil with that of standard crushed rock. Engineers use it to judge how well soil can support load under a road and a higher value generally means a stronger subgrade. In terms of CBR at the 85th percentile, chemical treatment of the subgrade resulted in in-situ values of CBR that ranged from 24 to 59. The corresponding value of soil beneath the layer of treated soil was only two. Hence, treated soil gave results that were about 12 to 30 times better than those of untreated soil. A falling weight deflectometer was also used to determine how the pavement behaved under load. Back-calculated modulus values for the treated layers were about twice those of the untreated soil.Most road sections remained in good conditionAdditionally, pavement condition status was considered along with soil strength test results. Twelve out of 14 roadways had pavements in good condition, according to Kentucky Transportation Cabinet criteria. The research team projected that these pavements would still be rated good at the end of their 20-year design period. Two roadways had a thin overlay of asphalt pavement after about 15 years. There was a difference in the soil layer condition as well. The untreated subgrade had a soft, moisture-affected surface layer, while the treated soils did not. This contributed to the better engineering characteristics of the chemically stabilised materials.Findings supported the long-term value of soil stabilisationThe study offered proof in the field that chemical improvement of road foundations would last through many years of use. The research included data from multiple locations with various stabilisers. This enabled the engineering personnel to evaluate the effectiveness of treatment through the test period rather than short laboratory tests. The research team also developed structural layer coefficients for estimating the load-carrying capacity of pavements built over chemically treated foundations. The values were tested using sections of the roads that were designed with thinner pavement.The research indicated that stabilisation of the road helped in maintaining the structural integrity of the road foundation. This does not imply that all treatments would be equally effective. Main factors such as composition of soil, moisture content, methods of construction and traffic loading have an impact on performance. The study helped transportation departments understand that the benefits of soil stabilization would last long after the construction process. It might also provide the designers of pavement structures with more design options.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Prince William added a microplastic filter to his home’s washing machine; the installer says he turned up in his socks
articles.summary: Prince William takes a stand against microplastic pollution by installing a washing machine filter at his home in Windsor, showcasing his commitment to the environment. Learn about this innovative technology and its impact.
articles.body: Most people probably never wonder where the fluff from their clothes goes after a wash. Prince William did. According to People magazine, the Prince of Wales had a microplastic filter installed on the washing machine at Forest Lodge, his family home in Windsor. Adam Root, founder and chief executive of Matter, the company that makes the filter, is the magazine’s source. Root said that while he and one of his colleagues were working on installation, the royal turned up in his socks, holding a cup of tea.The prince in his socksRoot and one of his colleagues were behind the washing machine, pulling things apart, when the prince walked in. Root described it as a very special moment and a real one. The Matter founder also mentioned that William was very firm about not taking any discount on the purchase of the filters and bought filters for his homes at full price. In his opinion, William’s concern for the environment is not a short-term thing. All of this comes from Root’s account and should be read as his version of the events.From Bristol to Windsor The Windsor installation was not William’s first encounter with the company. The Independent reported that he was genuinely horrified when he was shown a bottle of fibres collected from just 10 washes in a home machine on a previous trip to Matter’s headquarters in Bristol. Earlier reports also said William had the filters fitted at Kensington Palace and Anmer Hall, his country home in Norfolk. He was eager for the wider royal household to follow his example. Root says Matter has now sold its filters to nine royal palaces and plans to fit Buckingham Palace too.How Matter reached the royal laundry room William's connection to Matter comes from the Earthshot Prize, the environmental award he launched in 2020. The prize gives £1 million annually to five projects. Matter, based in Bristol, was a 2025 finalist in the Revive Our Oceans category. The magazine described it as an environmental technology company focused on capturing and recycling microplastics. Its filter gets attached to the exterior part of a washing machine. The Earthshot Prize’s profile of Matter said the self-cleaning device captures up to 97% of microplastic fibres without replacement cartridges. This is a claim about the product, not a result from some study. During the Bristol visit, Root told the prince that Matter employed around 50 people and was focused on fighting the growing problem of microplastic pollution.What research says about laundry fibres Why do washing machines need a filter at all? In a 2016 paper in the journal Marine Pollution Bulletin, Imogen Napper and Richard Thompson of Plymouth University estimated that an average 6 kg load of acrylic could release over 700,000 fibres. The authors said that washing clothes could be an important source of microplastics in water habitats. As to whether filters work, Lisa Erdle and team at the University of Toronto, in a 2021 Frontiers in Marine Science study, installed filters in 97 homes in Parry Sound, Ontario. The authors found that the town’s treated wastewater had a significant reduction in microfibers, an average of 41%. The study used a different filter, the Filtrol 160, so it doesn't prove Matter’s product works the same way. However, Erdle and colleagues said built-in filters in new machines are the way to go. One royal washing machine probably isn't going to fix microplastic pollution around the world. But the story gives an easy question to ask when people go shopping for their next machine.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella praises Jensen Huang but makes it clear that tech founders are not gods: ‘I used to tell Bill Gates…’
articles.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has weighed in on the cult of personality surrounding Silicon Valley founders, praising Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang for
articles.body: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has weighed in on the cult of personality surrounding Silicon Valley founders, praising Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang for building an enduring company while reminding the tech world that founders, like Microsoft’s Bill Gates, are human and not gods. Speaking about the outsized influence individual entrepreneurs have on their companies, Nadella acknowledged that founders deserve celebration for doing something almost magical: creating something out of nothing. However, he pushed back against the extreme hero worship often seen in modern tech and capitalism.“So therefore, yes, they're singular. But they're not gods, right?. So I kind of feel at the end of the day, you know, as you know, I used to say to Bill [Gates] and everyone, like, founders also die,” Nadella said.Satya Nadella on why lasting companies need more than one leaderIn Nadella’s view, a founder’s real legacy isn't just the initial spark they bring to a business, but whether the organisation can stand on its own feet once they step away. For any company to succeed over the long haul, someone else eventually has to take the reins.“So, at some point, a company needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over and, in fact, the person who is going to be most happy about that will be the founder, because when the baby you sort of brought into the world is striving long after you're gone. That's really the institutional strength you build,” he explained.Nadella made it clear that he has little patience for executives who claim a business fell apart simply because they left.“I have never trusted any leader, founder or otherwise, who comes and says the institution after I left was completely gone. I mean, what the heck? Like, then what did you build?” he remarked.Satya Nadella credits Jensen Huang’s work at NvidiaAccording to Nadella, true greatness in leadership comes down to balancing two things: the “magic” a founder creates at the start and the lasting “institutional strength” they leave behind.Pointing to Nvidia as a prime example of getting that balance right, Nadella credited Huang with building a resilient organisation capable of outlasting its founder. “And so I think that's what Jensen actually has done with Nvidia,” Nadella said.However, he stopped short of endorsing a potential comeback for the Nvidia co-founder. “I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it's not up to me. It's up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next,” Nadella said, adding that he has “all the admiration, respect for what Jensen has done for this industry, and what he's done for Nvidia, noting that the two have worked together for many years.”Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Portugal deployed seven artificial reef systems across 43.5 sq km off the Algarve; a study using 27 years of data estimated seabream carrying capacity rose 35%, or 895 tonnes
articles.summary: Discover how Portugal's artificial reefs off the Algarve have increased seabream carrying capacity by 35%, supporting fish population growth and biodiversity over 27 years, while also influencing fishing practices.
articles.body: Can people build a better home for fish? Portugal gave it a try. A 2008 symposium paper by Gianna Fabi and colleagues stated that seven artificial reef systems were deployed in the Algarve, in southern Portugal. They spanned 43.5 square kilometres of seabed. The paper said the reefs had successfully improved fishing yields and made catches more diverse. Then a later study asked a sharper question: did the reefs only attract fish or did they help create more of them?Why build homes for fish underwater Artificial reefs refer to the man-made structures that are placed on the seabed. They can be thought of like apartments for fish. The same research paper observed that artificial reefs have been created in the western Mediterranean basin since 1960. In the Mediterranean, the countries that have been involved include France, Italy, Spain, and Monaco. Portugal built its reefs on its Atlantic coast. The main goal had mostly been to protect and boost fishing resources used by recreational and commercial fishers. The authors added that these reefs often serve several purposes at the same time. Some also help protect natural habitats such as seagrass beds that serve as nurseries for young fish.A huge reef project off the Algarve The Algarve project was big. The paper described it as a large complex of seven artificial reef systems. They included more than 20,950 modules that weighed 73,000 tonnes in total. Their combined volume was 103,000 cubic metres. The reefs reportedly increased biodiversity and the amount of life living on the seabed. They also became a popular site for recreational diving and research.Did the reefs make fish or just attract them?Fish can just swim over to the reef from other places. This would mean higher catches without adding any new fish to the sea. Scientists called this the attraction hypothesis. The other theory is that of the production hypothesis, where the reefs increase the overall fish population. According to Ruben Roa-Ureta and team, before this paper, it had not been established which hypothesis was right. Their 2019 paper, ‘Modelling long-term fisheries data to resolve the attraction versus production dilemma of artificial reefs,’ published in Ecological Modelling, tried to settle the debate.What 27 years of data revealed The team looked at the two-banded seabream in the south of Portugal. They used monthly records of 27 years of landings and 20 years of fishing effort for three fleets. One small-scale fleet fished on the reefs, while two semi-industrial fleets worked the broader continental shelf. They then calculated regional carrying capacity, the number of fish an area can support. If fish had only moved, it would have been constant. Instead, the authors found it increased by 35% after the final reefs were dropped. It went up straight for four years. This, the authors said, challenged the idea of attraction. A later review in Frontiers in Marine Science estimated the rise at around 895 tonnes.The catch behind the good news There is, however, a twist. The study found the reefs helped the artisanal fisheries by increasing stock biomass. However, fishing pressure rose as well. The harvest rate of the semi-industrial fleets working offshore increased to almost three times its previous level. This resulted in a large increase in total fish mortality and the rate of exploitation. The result was more layered than just a simple success story. The study also focused on one species in one region, so it cannot represent all the reefs around the world. But Ruben Roa-Ureta and colleagues said their method could be used elsewhere since it only needs basic fishing data.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: More than 100,000 strangers have shared handwritten stories anonymously; what do their confessions reveal about loneliness, grief, love and hope?
articles.summary: “My family needs this exhibit,” said a stranger. “Life has felt like a beautiful thriller,” said another.
articles.body: “My family needs this exhibit,” said a stranger. “Life has felt like a beautiful thriller,” said another. Some parts of our lives, the most dangerous and guarded corners of our worlds, are often the easiest to reach into when we know we may be heard, seen or, in the case of The Strangers Project, read.Stories have travelled far and wide since the beginning of time. Words have been caught between strange worlds, woven by strangers, making their way into myths, orature and, most often, simply explaining the absurdities of life itself. But why, in a world of notes apps, comments and chat boxes, do we yearn to disperse ourselves in ink on paper? Why must we write, and why must we remember?Brandon Doman first started the project in 2009 with a simple idea: to collect stories, something palpable and tangible, shared by hand on a page, always in person and always anonymously. Today, with the project having gathered over 100,000 stories, the world is met with a living repository. It is an art installation of what it is simply to be human, and of the condition we are all ridden with: life. You can now find Doman collecting stories from Thursday to Sunday, between 2 and 6:30 pm, at the project's semi-installation at the World Trade Center Oculus in New York City, USA.“Exploring the lives of the people we share space with every day shows us how wonderfully human we all are. These stories engage strangers of all ages and backgrounds to reflect, rejoice, heal and connect through words,” Doman writes on the project's website.“You cannot practice love with someone you don’t love,” writes someone who has visited The Strangers Project wall for the fifth time. As life has changed, so has their perspective on love, and the words seem almost like a reminder to slowly bandage a hurting, broken heart that is beginning to heal. Some confessions are written to speak to parts of who we once were when we were in love, as we struggle with the little griefs that accompany it. Because while remembering may hurt too much, being reminded can feel almost necessary, like a repair, a fix.“I have a dream to be a singer and I will not let haters bring me down!” writes a girl from Toronto. Written with equal parts courage and kindness, the confession carries the yearning of a heart holding on to a dream. Some dreams necessitate a fire within us, a determination to keep going, and an insatiable hunger even when the world may not always be kind. And so, anonymously as it may be, this is a little declaration of hope, written down for the world to read.“I forgive you. I know you raised me the best you could. As a Black man, I know being vulnerable was hard for you,” writes a son to his father. Growing up in a world that demands so much of you, especially because of how you identify, can shape the relationships you carry with you. In these words, a son seems to wrestle with the challenges of the father he had and the son he now chooses to be.“I lost my Best Friend…TELL THEM ‘I LOVE YOU’. SAY I LOVE YOU before it is too late.” Across these pages, you find smatterings of feelings left unsaid. While one person writes to forgive, another is still remembering, holding on to words that perhaps never found their way to the person they were meant for. So writes a grieving person, with love that is immense and grief that clings and refuses to leave. While this pain tends to follow us, its imprint may take the shape of love. When your heart aches for what you have lost, perhaps you can still find your way back to the love you have, especially on the days you forget to put it into words.“I feel some freedom knowing we are all in this together, and knowing how minor most things are in the scope of history, our life’s journey, let alone the history of humankind!” There is a certain freedom in knowing that, despite the different lives we lead and the different things we carry, we are all part of something much larger. Our worries, our griefs, our little triumphs and our dreams may feel like the entirety of our worlds when we are living through them, but somewhere, in another corner of the world, someone else is feeling, remembering and hoping too.In big, black, bold letters, the words “This space is for you” spread across the project’s site, where you are instantly acknowledged and spoken to. While some of us yearn to be seen, others wish to shrink, hide or slowly dissipate. The project’s space, by design, rushes to embrace you, gently nudging you to sit with whatever you may be feeling.Despite the different people we may be, our life stories can tether us to the people we may never meet, see or hear, but whose lives will compel us to look at our own. articles.title: A flaw in the granite forced workers to abandon Thomas Jefferson’s original position on Mount Rushmore; they moved him to the other side of Washington
articles.summary: Discover the unexpected challenges faced during the construction of Mount Rushmore, including how a granite flaw led to Thomas Jefferson's relocation and the changes made to the monument's design.
articles.body: Mount Rushmore might look like a plan that went perfectly, but the road to getting there wasn't without hiccups. The National Park Service’s page on the Entablature idea reads that in 1934, the Thomas Jefferson figure was moved from Washington's right (the viewer’s left) to his left due to inconsistencies in the rock. That one flaw in the granite didn’t just move one face; it ended up changing the entire plan for the mountain.A mountain carved with dynamite The carving ran from 4 October 1927 to 31 October 1941. According to the National Park Service’s Carving History Page, nearly 400 men and women worked on the project. Blasting was a big part of the process. About 90% of the mountain was carved using dynamite. Powdermen would cut and place specific-sized charges to remove specific amounts of rock. The process continued until there were three to six inches of rock remaining. Then drillers and assistant carvers made holes very close to each other in the granite surface. This process is called honeycombing, and it helped weaken the rock so it could be manually removed. Workers were lowered over the 500-foot-tall surface of the mountain in a bosun’s chair. Even though it was risky, no fatal accidents were reported during the 14 years of construction.Plan changes as Jefferson movesSculptor Gutzon Borglum reportedly had big plans for the mountain. He wanted a large inscription there, the Entablature, along with the faces of the four presidents. It was supposed to be a short history of the United States, carved in letters three feet high. The inscription was planned to sit in an area shaped like the Louisiana Purchase territory. The park service suggests that the inscription was meant to present Mount Rushmore as a national memorial to the country's first 150 years, and not just the lives of four great men. Work started, and in 1930, the year 1776 was carved into the east side of the mountain.In 1934, however, Jefferson had to be moved from the right side of Washington to his left because of the inconsistencies in the rock. This brought on further changes along the way. The spot set for the Entablature had to be taken up by Lincoln. Borglum also said that the words would be too hard to read from below. So, the plan changed again. Now the history would go into the Hall of Records, a room behind the sculpture. But Borglum died in 1941, before the plans for the inscription could be finalised.The essay contestThe plan was for Calvin Coolidge to write the history of the United States. But there were disagreements between Coolidge and Borglum on how it should be worded. Coolidge passed away in 1933 before the wording could be finalised. In 1934, Borglum teamed up with the Hearst newspapers to sponsor an essay contest. The winning words were supposed to be carved somewhere on the mountain alongside the four presidents. Once the winners were announced and the prizes awarded, Borglum decided against carving anything into his monument.There was one winner who left a strong impression. A young Nebraskan named William Andrew Burkett won the college-age category. He wrote his essay when he was a student at the Omaha University Law School in 1934. Burkett donated a bronze plaque of his essay on 4 July 1971. The plaque now hangs on the Borglum View Terrace, which was the site of the first studio at Mount Rushmore. The story shows how even a famous landmark was shaped by setbacks that are often lost in the pages of history.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 48-year-old Jersey City woman who says a New Jersey trooper handcuffed her while she was having a stroke won $11.25 million, and the state is now asking an appeals court to throw out the verdict
articles.summary: What was meant to be a routine morning commute turned into a life-changing medical emergency for a New Jersey woman who was left battling for her life
articles.body: What was meant to be a routine morning commute turned into a life-changing medical emergency for a New Jersey woman who was left battling for her life after the very people who were supposed to help her, allegedly mistook her stroke symptoms for signs of intoxication. It was followed by a disastrous delay in medical treatment that left her permanently disabled and needing round-the-clock care. Years later, she was awarded millions in damages by a jury. But the state is now pushing back against that decision, arguing the trooper who made the arrest shouldn’t be legally liable for it.Drunkenness posing as a medical emergencyAccording to The Independent, Cheryl Lynn Rhines was driving from her home in Jersey City to her job in Florham Park on October 17, 2017. The 48-year-old is a senior marketing executive for German chemical firm BASF. While driving along the New Jersey Turnpike extension, she suddenly developed signs of a severe stroke.Rhines pulled over near Interstate 78 in Newark as she deteriorated. Her car finally hit a guardrail along the road and kept going.Court documents cited by The Independent say New Jersey State Police troopers arrived about 30 minutes later. They said they found Rhines having trouble communicating and showing clear physical signs such as facial droop, trouble moving and confusion.She said in her lawsuit the stroke impacted the right side of her body, making it difficult for her to follow instructions or control the vehicle. She was also said to be unable to speak properly and only able to give limited answers. Trooper Jennifer Albuja, however, suspected Rhines was under the influence of some unknown substance.Get handcuffed instead of emergency treatmentAccording to The Independent, Rhines was taken out of her car, handcuffed and taken into police custody instead of going straight to the hospital.Her attorneys said the trooper did not realize how serious her medical condition was, given numerous visible signs of a stroke. The lawsuit also claimed officers said Rhines was being uncooperative and suggested she was purposely making things difficult.The Independent reported that Rhines allegedly struggled to keep herself under control as she was thrown onto the hood of her car. Her lawyers also said she had bruises on her arms, knee and shin that were noted when she was finally given medical treatment.Instead of being taken to a nearby emergency stroke center, Rhines ended up at the New Jersey State Police barracks in Somerville. Emergency medical personnel were only called when someone at the station saw her condition.The delay cost Rhines about two and a half crucial hours where she might have had urgent stroke treatment, The Independent reported.Late treatment leading to permanent disabilityThe results of the delay in medical care were catastrophic, the report says. Medical professionals were eventually able to break up the blood clot in Rhines’ brain, but the damage had already been done.The Independent said the delay caused “substantial brain injury” and “permanent disability.” Rhines was left with constant difficulties of communication and was unable to continue with her professional career, needing ongoing assistance with daily tasks.In her lawsuit, she contended the officers should have realized she needed immediate medical attention and called for emergency services instead of treating her condition as a possible criminal matter.The case also raised wider issues about police training, emergency response procedures and the duty of officers when confronted with people showing signs of serious medical conditions.Jury awards $11 million-plus in damagesThe lawsuit ultimately resulted in a huge monetary award. NJ reports that an Essex County jury awarded damages of about $19.1 million in January 2025.But the jury also determined that some of Rhines' injuries were caused by the delay in treatment, reducing the award to about $11.46 million. Further adjustments brought the final judgment to approximately $11.25 million.Superior Court Judge Thomas Vena denied the state’s request for a new trial in April 2025, allowing the judgment to stand.Verdict appeals New JerseyThe state is now trying to overturn the judgment before a three-judge panel of the Appellate Division in Trenton. New Jersey filed its appeal in October 2025, stating that Albuja had acted in good faith because Rhines’ slurred speech, disorientation and inability to stand reasonably suggested possible intoxication, NJ report said.The state says the trooper should be immune from prosecution for her actions. Or it has asked for a new trial or a reduction in the damages awarded.Another important point is the jury instructions and the calculation of damages. The state argues that awarding separate damages for pain and suffering and emotional distress could have resulted in Rhines being compensated twice for overlapping injuries.Her attorneys have disputed that position, saying the emotional trauma of being restrained and allegedly denied medical aid was separate from the lasting effects of her brain injury.According to NJ, Rhines' attorneys also argue that the trooper had a duty to call for medical assistance before making an arrest, especially since the woman showed signs of having a stroke.Now it is up to the appeals court to decide whether to uphold the original finding of liability and the award of damages. To Rhines, the legal battle is just another chapter in a tragedy that began on a routine morning commute and changed the course of her life forever.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.body: Seven people were killed in a clash between two tribes over the ownership of a forest in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, news agency PTI reported, quoting police Saturday.The incident took place around 10pm local time on Thursday at Bilija forest in Battagram district, when armed members of the Gilal and Kaloch tribes confronted each other, leading to an exchange of gunfire.According to police, armed men from the Kaloch tribe took positions and opened fire, prompting retaliation from the Gilal side. Four members of the Gilal tribe and three from the Kaloch tribe were killed in the clash.The two tribes have been involved in a longstanding dispute over the ownership of Bilija forest, which has continued for several decades and claimed several lives in the past, police said.The Gilal tribe is associated with the Allai valley in Battagram district, while the Kaloch community belongs to neighbouring Kohistan district.Police said repeated efforts by the administrations of both districts to resolve the dispute and bring the communities together had failed to produce a permanent solution.The latest clash has once again raised concerns over the law and order situation in Imran Khan's stronghold Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.You use AI every day. articles.title: China-Pakistan ties raise two-front conflict risk for India: US report
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A US congressional commission has warned that China's growing military partnership with Pakistan is increasing the risk of a two-front security
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A US congressional commission has warned that China's growing military partnership with Pakistan is increasing the risk of a two-front security challenge for India. It has urged Washington to deepen operational defence cooperation with New Delhi, particularly in the Indian Ocean region, news agency ANI cited report.In its report, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC) said Beijing's expanding military and security support for Islamabad had made the possibility of a two-front conflict an increasingly pressing concern for India.In a chapter titled "China’s Other Front: India and the Future of US Strategy in the Indo-Pacific," the commission examined China's growing strategic presence in South Asia and its implications for India's security and the broader regional balance of power.Referring to the May 2025 India-Pakistan military conflict, which followed the Islamabad-sponsored Pahalgam terror attack that killed 26 people, the report said the episode highlighted how China could support Pakistan during a crisis without directly entering the conflict.India had launched Operation Sindoor in response to the attack, targeting terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.The commission said China's backing for Pakistan could complicate India's military planning and increase the challenges it would face in any future conflict with its western neighbour.According to the report, Beijing views India's growing influence as a strategic challenge and uses military, economic and maritime pressure to limit its rise. It also described India as one of the few countries outside the US alliance system with the demographic, economic, military and geographic strength to influence the long-term balance of power with China.Highlighting India's position as the world's most populous country, largest democracy and a nuclear-armed state with one of the world's largest militaries, the commission pointed to its strategic geography. India shares a 2,100-mile contested border with China and is located along key Indian Ocean sea lanes that carry a significant share of China's energy supplies and trade.While the Western Pacific remains the main arena of US-China rivalry, the report said India presents Beijing with another strategic challenge, both on land and at sea.However, the commission also acknowledged that India's approach to China is driven by its own strategic interests and commitment to "strategic autonomy". It cautioned that stronger India-US ties would not necessarily mean New Delhi would align with Washington on every broader foreign policy objective.For Washington, the report said, a stronger India could help create a more favourable balance of power in Asia and provide an alternative to China in manufacturing and global supply chains.China's growing presence in Indian OceanThe report also flagged China's expanding naval and surveillance presence in the Indian Ocean, saying it could test India's traditional strategic advantages in the region and place additional operational pressure on its armed forces.It said Beijing was developing infrastructure and logistical support to sustain longer naval deployments, while Chinese naval, surveillance and research vessels were operating closer to India and strategically important sea lanes.The commission further said China was applying elements of its South China Sea approach to the Indian Ocean. It cited Beijing's references to historic rights and the renaming of undersea features, which it said could lay the groundwork for more assertive actions or potential jurisdictional claims in the region.To counter China's growing presence, the commission recommended that the US Congress direct the US secretary of defence and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff to work with India to strengthen undersea and maritime domain awareness across the Indian Ocean.It called for cooperation to move beyond periodic military exercises towards more sustained operational coordination. This could include regular intelligence and surveillance sharing, joint tracking of Chinese naval and submarine movements, and better procedures to respond to maritime threats.The report also recommended setting up an Indo-American Strategic Leadership Exchange Program to develop long-term connections among emerging defence, government, business and academic leaders from the two countries.India-China ties and boundary disputeThe report's observations come amid efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to stabilise bilateral ties and address their longstanding border dispute.Earlier in September, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping met on the sidelines of the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi. The two leaders expressed commitment to finding a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution to the boundary question and agreed that bilateral relations should be viewed from a strategic and long-term perspective.According to the MEA, the leaders "reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties." PM Modi emphasised that "differences should not become disputes" and that both sides must be guided by "mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest."The prime minister also stressed that peace and tranquillity along the border remained essential for the continued development of bilateral relations. He underlined the need for both countries to follow existing agreements and understandings on border-related issues."The two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question proceeding from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relations and the long-term interests of the two peoples," the MEA said.Xi said India and China should view their relationship from a strategic perspective and keep the long-term development of bilateral ties in mind. He added that although the two countries were different, they had been able to "support and help each other to achieve common development."The Chinese president also highlighted the shared position of India and China as the world's most populous countries and members of the Global South, saying both had important responsibilities in advancing a shared future for humanity.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Bangladesh wage protests: Clashes erupt between garment workers and police, dozens of factories shut
articles.summary: Tensions escalated in Bangladesh's Ashulia on Saturday as garment workers demanding a hike in minimum wages clashed with security forces.
articles.body: Tensions escalated in Bangladesh's Ashulia on Saturday as garment workers demanding a hike in minimum wages clashed with security forces. Police fired tear gas to disperse the protesters and bring the situation under control, The Daily Star reported.According to the news agency ANI, the confrontation took place around 11 am in the Kathgara area along the Zirabo-Bismail road. Workers from several garment factories had stopped production and joined the protest, according to the report.Eyewitnesses told The daily star that workers at multiple factories in Kathgara first entered their workplaces before stopping work. They later organised a rally and attempted to block the road around 10:45 am after factory management announced holidays.Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police at industrial police-1 in Ashulia, said in a text message around noon that the situation had returned to normal."Some unruly workers were trying to create instability at the garment factories that remained operational in the Kathgara area. Industrial police and other forces intervened to keep the situation under control," Bhuiyan said.Earlier on Saturday, at least 50 factories in the Savar-Ashulia industrial belt announced holidays following work stoppages. However, most factories in the area had started operations as usual in the morning, industrial police told the newspaper.The latest clashes come amid continuing protests by garment workers across Bangladesh over demands for higher wages and better working conditions.On Tuesday, garment workers staged demonstrations in Mirpur, Dhaka, demanding that the minimum monthly wage be increased to 30,000 taka. The protests came as labour unrest spread across the country's textile industry, forcing several factories to suspend operations.Protesters also attempted to block roads but were stopped by police, who intervened to prevent traffic disruptions and maintain law and order.Garment workers in several parts of Bangladesh have been staging strikes to demand better pay, with demonstrations leading to factory closures in multiple industrial areas, DW reported.Separately, a group of workers gathered at Padmar Mor in the Hemayetpur area of Savar around 3 pm on Monday, briefly disrupting the area. Police asked them to disperse peacefully, following which they cleared the road without further incident, Dhaka Tribune reported.Meanwhile, around 40 factories remained closed in the Savar and Ashulia industrial zones on Monday, according to industrial police.Of these, 27 factories were shut under section 13(1) of the Bangladesh labour act, while nine were declared closed indefinitely. The remaining factories observed general holidays.Bhuiyan said workers at one factory refused to resume work after the lunch break and continued sitting inside the premises, prompting management to declare a holiday. Employees at two other factories also stopped work and staged sit-in protests inside their workplaces.However, workers at other factories across the industrial areas continued their operations peacefully, he added.You use AI every day. articles.title: Atlanta BeltLine adds 37-foot quilt-inspired sculpture to Southside Trail, designed by two local artists to reflect surrounding communities
articles.summary: Atlanta’s BeltLine has added a 37-foot-tall sculpture inspired by traditional quilts to its Southside Trail, creating a new landmark near Pittsburgh Yards.
articles.body: Atlanta’s BeltLine has added a 37-foot-tall sculpture inspired by traditional quilts to its Southside Trail, creating a new landmark near Pittsburgh Yards. Called “Quilts in the Sky”, the installation was created by Atlanta artists Marryam Moma and Adana Tillman and designed with the surrounding neighbourhoods and trail users in mind. The sculpture is the first major public art installation on the newly completed Southside Trail, which runs 1.9 miles from Pittsburgh Yards to Boulevard. According to the Atlanta BeltLine, the three-dimensional work combines Tillman’s textile and quilting practice with Moma’s analog collage techniques, using colourful plexiglass pieces arranged to resemble a traditional quilt.37-foot ‘Quilts in the Sky’ sculpture joins Atlanta BeltLine’s Southside TrailThe sculpture stands where the Southside Trail meets Pittsburgh Yards and measures 37 feet by 15 feet. Axios reported that it is the first major art installation on the trail segment, which opened in June 2026 and connects Pittsburgh Yards with Boulevard.The Atlanta BeltLine said “Quilts in the Sky” brings together Tillman’s work as a textile artist and Moma’s collage practice in a three-dimensional structure. Colourful plexiglass pieces form quilt-like patterns, creating a large-scale interpretation of traditional quilt designs.The installation was commissioned after Tillman was selected through Atlanta BeltLine Art’s annual open call for artists in 2024. She later partnered with Moma to develop the project, with artist and fabricator Antonio Darden supporting fabrication and Soco Contracting Company and Bonsai assisting with installation.Local artists designed sculpture around nearby Atlanta communitiesMoma and Tillman developed the sculpture specifically with the communities around the Southside Trail in mind. The trail links neighbourhoods including Peoplestown, Chosewood Park, Boulevard Heights, Capitol View Manor and the Villages at Carver.The Atlanta BeltLine said the artists wanted the piece to represent joy and create a place where people could gather and spend time together. Tillman also said the intention was for future installations to reflect the distinct identities of the communities where they are placed.The project also builds on the artists’ involvement in Atlanta BeltLine programmes supporting local creatives. Moma took part in the inaugural Beltline Business Ventures: Artists Edition cohort in 2024, while Tillman graduated from the programme’s second cohort in 2026. The initiative provides artists with business training and resources to help them develop their practices and pursue larger public art opportunities.“Quilts in the Sky” is part of Atlanta Beltline Art’s broader public art programme, which has commissioned artists across disciplines for more than 16 years. The programme aims to bring works shaped by the history, character and creative traditions of neighbourhoods along the BeltLine.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Gurgaon man orders Rs 28,814 bookcase from Insaraf.com, termite-like powder emerges, replacement never comes; consumer commission orders refund with 9% interest, Rs 25,000 compensation and costs
articles.summary: GURGAON: An online furniture buyer who found termite-like powder emerging from a wooden bookcase and was promised a replacement that never arrived has
articles.body: GURGAON: An online furniture buyer who found termite-like powder emerging from a wooden bookcase and was promised a replacement that never arrived has been awarded more than Rs 53,800 by a Gurgaon consumer commission, which held the seller guilty of deficiency in service.The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission directed Saraf Furniture, which operates the online platform Insaraf.com, to refund Rs 28,814.15 paid for the furniture, along with 9% annual interest from the date of purchase. It also ordered the company to pay Rs 15,000 compensation for mental harassment and Rs 10,000 towards litigation expenses.Mohan Bansiwal, a resident of Sector 43, Gurgaon, had purchased a solid-wood bookcase/study wardrobe through the company's online platform on October 27, 2024, for Rs 28,814.15. He alleged that within days of receiving the furniture, white powder-like residue began emerging from it, indicating termite infestation.The product, however, was sold with a promise of lifetime warranty against wood termites and a 12-month warranty against manufacturing defects, according to the complaint.Bansiwal contacted the company on April 1, 2025, through telephone and email and shared photographs of the defective furniture. The company, in an email dated April 2, acknowledged the defect and assured him that a replacement would be shipped soon. However, the replacement never arrived, prompting him to seek a refund.After repeated emails failed to elicit a resolution, Bansiwal sent a legal notice on August 13, 2025, but the company did not respond. He subsequently approached the consumer commission, alleging deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.The commission noted that the company had been duly served but failed to appear before it and was proceeded against ex-parte. The consumer's affidavit, invoice, warranty terms, email correspondence, photographs and legal notice were placed on record.Observing that the complainant's evidence remained unrebutted and there was no reason to disbelieve it, the commission held the seller guilty of deficiency in service and allowed the complaint.The order, passed on November 11 by commission member Khushwinder Kaur, directed the company to pay the awarded amount within 45 days of the order. articles.title: Republican senator Tillis blocks Trump's CISA nominee after Jan 6 attack denial
articles.summary: US Senator Thom Tillis has put a hold on Michael LoSapio's nomination to lead CISA after LoSapio failed to acknowledge the Capitol attack on January 6, 2021, raising concerns about cybersecurity leadership amid rising tensions.
articles.body: US Senator Thom Tillis has blocked President Donald Trump's nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) after the candidate declined to acknowledge that the US Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021.Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina who is not seeking re-election, confirmed that he had placed a hold on Michael LoSapio's nomination. The move could prevent his appointment from being included in a package of nominations scheduled for a Senate vote next month.The dispute followed LoSapio's confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee on Thursday. During the session, Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut asked whether the Capitol had come under attack on January 6, 2021.“I, I don’t know,” LoSapio initially replied. When Blumenthal pressed him, the nominee said, “No, I don’t believe it was an attack.”Blumenthal gave him another opportunity to answer, asking directly whether the Capitol had been attacked that day. LoSapio again denied that it had, responding, “No, sir.”Tillis said the events of January 6 were not a matter of interpretation and criticised LoSapio's response.“It’s binary. The minute you pretend like it didn’t exist or you can’t even acknowledge it, I don’t have any time because it’s not a very thoughtful person,” Tillis told The Hill.LoSapio previously worked as an executive at technology company Palantir. His nomination has drawn attention because CISA is responsible for helping protect US critical infrastructure, including systems used to conduct elections.The agency played a prominent role after the 2020 presidential election, when it joined other federal bodies in rejecting claims of widespread voting system interference. In a joint statement issued the following week, election security officials described the vote as “the most secure in American history” and said there was no evidence that voting systems had deleted, lost or changed votes.Trump later targeted former CISA director Chris Krebs in an April 2025 presidential memorandum, accusing him of dismissing claims that the 2020 election had been rigged and stolen.The agency's leadership has also come under scrutiny following recent technical disruptions, including an outage affecting Microsoft Outlook and a nationwide ground stop imposed by the Federal Aviation Administration. Cybersecurity experts have said cyberattacks cannot be ruled out as a possible cause, although federal officials have not reported finding evidence of an attack.You use AI every day. articles.title: A New York woman says she lived in an apartment for 20 years, but the landlord required her company to sign a commercial lease for residential space; an appeals court has allowed her rent-stabilisation fight to continue
articles.summary: A New York landlord's attempt to recover possession of an apartment has suffered a setback after an appeals court allowed a long-running dispute over
articles.body: A New York landlord's attempt to recover possession of an apartment has suffered a setback after an appeals court allowed a long-running dispute over rent-stabilisation protections to proceed. The case centres on E. Terese Carpenter, who says she has lived in a Manhattan apartment for more than 20 years, even though the landlord required a company she owned to sign a commercial lease describing the space as being used exclusively for business. In a November 19, 2026 decision, available on Justia, the New York Supreme Court's Appellate Division, First Department, upheld a lower court's refusal to grant the landlord summary judgment, finding that there were unresolved questions about the apartment's actual residential use and the landlord's knowledge of it. The ruling in 38 E. 64th St., LLC v. Nile, Inc. allows Carpenter's rent-stabilisation claims to continue.Landlord sought to recover the Manhattan apartmentThe dispute involves an apartment in a building at 38 East 64th Street in Manhattan. The landlord, 38 East 64th Street, LLC, rented the unit to Nile, Inc., a company owned by Carpenter, beginning in or around 2006. Although the premises were an apartment, the landlord required Nile to enter into a commercial lease stating that the space would be used exclusively for business purposes. The building's certificate of occupancy, however, permitted only residential use.Carpenter maintained that she had always intended to use the apartment as her home and had actually lived there for more than two decades. The defendants argued that the landlord knew about and accepted this residential occupation despite the wording of the commercial lease. The landlord subsequently brought an action seeking possession of the apartment and payment for its use and occupancy. It also sought attorneys' fees under the lease agreement.Nile and Carpenter contested the action, arguing that the apartment remained subject to New York's Rent Stabilisation Law and that the commercial lease arrangement had been used to remove the unit improperly from rent regulation.Tenant challenges the commercial lease arrangementThe dispute raised an important question about whether the description of a property in a lease is enough to determine its legal status when the actual use of the premises is different. The defendants argued that Carpenter's long-term residential occupation, together with the landlord's knowledge and acceptance of that arrangement, meant that the apartment could still qualify for rent-stabilisation protections.They also brought counterclaims alleging that the landlord had illegally and fraudulently deregulated the unit. If established, their claims could entitle Carpenter to a court declaration recognising her as the lawful rent-stabilised tenant. The landlord, meanwhile, sought summary judgment in its favour and asked the court to dismiss the defendants' counterclaims and affirmative defences. In May 2025, New York County Supreme Court Justice Lyle E Frank denied the landlord's application. The landlord appealed that decision to the First Department.Appeals court finds questions about residential useThe Appellate Division examined whether the evidence raised factual questions that needed to be resolved before the landlord could obtain judgment without a trial. The judges noted that the defendants had submitted sufficient evidence to raise a question about whether the apartment was being used for residential purposes with the landlord's knowledge and acquiescence.The court referred to an earlier First Department ruling, Hadzovic v. Buckley School in the City of New York, which established that disputes involving mixed residential and commercial use must initially be resolved by a factfinder. It also noted that the landlord did not dispute the defendants' assertion that it had required them to sign a commercial lease exclusively for business use, despite the building's certificate of occupancy allowing only residential occupation.Furthermore, the landlord had failed to provide evidence contradicting Carpenter's claim that she had always intended to live in the apartment and had actually done so for more than 20 years. The court also found that the defendants had sufficiently stated their counterclaims concerning the apartment's rent-stabilised status and alleged illegal deregulation.Landlord's appeal unanimously rejectedOn November 19, 2026, the First Department unanimously affirmed the lower court's order, without costs. This means the landlord did not obtain the summary judgment or dismissal of the defendants' claims it had sought. However, the ruling does not finally establish that Carpenter is a rent-stabilised tenant or that the landlord illegally deregulated the apartment. Those issues remain to be determined through further proceedings.The decision means that the commercial lease cannot, by itself, end the dispute over the apartment's residential use and potential rent-stabilised status. Carpenter and Nile can continue pursuing their claims, while the landlord's action to recover possession and use and occupancy remains unresolved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 1913, Ohio parents found their 10-pound baby fit under the new 11-pound Parcel Post limit; they sent James Beagle to his grandmother for 15 cents, insured him for $50, and a rural mail carrier delivered him safely
articles.summary: In 1913, an Ohio couple found a practical answer to a simple family problem.
articles.body: In 1913, an Ohio couple found a practical answer to a simple family problem. Their eight month old son, James Beagle, weighed just under the new 11 pound Parcel Post limit, so they sent him to his grandmother in nearby Batavia for 15 cents in postage and insured him for $50, according to Futura Sciences, the Smithsonian National Postal Museum, and the U.S. Postal Service.Rural Free Delivery carrier Vernon Lytle carried James about a mile to his grandmother’s home. The trip became one of the earliest known cases of a child being sent through the U.S. mail, though it looked very different from the image of a baby packed in a mailbag. Read more about this unusual incident, as per the reports, here:Why the family used the mailParcel Post began on January 1, 1913. It expanded the kinds of packages Americans could send and gave rural households easier access to mail order goods.In its early years, customers and postal officials were still learning how the service could be used. Some families saw it as a cheaper alternative to a train ticket when they needed to send a child to a relative. And so, the Beagle family’s case was not about putting a child in a sack. James travelled with a trusted local carrier who knew the route and the family.How the delivery workedJames was carried by Vernon Lytle, a Rural Free Delivery carrier. The trip covered only about a mile, from the Beagle home in Glen Este to his grandmother’s house in Batavia. The parents paid 15 cents for postage and insured their son for $50. James was delivered safely, and the story attracted attention because it was unusual and, in the words of Smithsonian historian Jenny Lynch, “probably because it was so cute.”The case became known as the first documented example of a child being sent through the mail in the United States. It was followed by other cases in Pennsylvania, Idaho, Maryland, Florida, Missouri, and Kentucky.Why it did not lastThe Post Office Department moved quickly to close the loophole. After May Pierstorff’s trip in 1914 and a separate inquiry about mailing children, Postmaster General Albert Burleson directed postmasters to bar all human beings from the mail, the reports suggest.Despite the ban, some rural carriers continued to transport children. In March 1914, a Maryland carrier carried a 14 pound baby 12 miles from Clear Spring to Indian Springs. In 1915, six year old Edna Neff travelled by railway mail train from Pensacola, Florida, to Christianburg, Virginia. Her trip cost 15 cents, and she weighed just under the 50 pound Parcel Post limit.What the cases showThe stories show how rural communities relied on postal workers they knew. Carriers often served isolated households and were seen as trusted links between neighbours and family members. The cases also reflect the uncertainty around a new service. Parcel Post opened up new possibilities, but the rules had not yet caught up with every possible use.The final known case involved three year old Maud Smith in 1915. After that, postal officials investigated the trip, and the practice appears to have ended.What the story means todayToday, the idea of mailing a child sounds alarming. But the historical record shows that these were not cases of children being packed and shipped like parcels. They were cases of parents using a new service in a way that made sense at the time to them. The children travelled with trusted carriers, and the trips were often short.The U.S. Postal Service now makes clear that children cannot be sent through the mail. The early Parcel Post cases remain a strange but fascinating chapter in the history of American delivery.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Bullets rain from helicopter, explosions on ground: How Mexico hunted down FBI's most-wanted drug lord; watch
articles.summary: The capture of one of the FBI's 10 most-wanted fugitives triggered a fierce gun battle in Mexico's Sinaloa state on Friday, turning an elite military
articles.body: The capture of one of the FBI's 10 most-wanted fugitives triggered a fierce gun battle in Mexico's Sinaloa state on Friday, turning an elite military operation into a night of chaos. As helicopters opened fire from above and explosions rocked the ground, armed militants mounted a counterattack, setting up roadblocks across nearby areas.The violence even reached a baseball stadium in Guasave, where players abandoned the match and fans scrambled for cover. Mexican authorities said alleged cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores was arrested in an operation carried out with US assistance.How the operation unfoldedMexico's defence ministry said the operation was carried out by "elite military forces" using "stealth and surprise" to reach Meza-Flores, who is also known as "El Chapo Isidro". He leads the Guasave-based Meza-Flores criminal organisation, also known as Los Mazatlecos.The operation, however, met armed resistance. The defence ministry said authorities "came under attack with gunfire and explosives" after launching the operation. Militants also set up roadblocks in several municipalities near the arrest site.Footage showed what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters circling over Guasave and firing rapidly towards the ground. Another surveillance video showed an apparent exchange of gunfire between cartel members travelling in a truck and military helicopters, CNN reported.Local authorities confirmed "an attack on federal personnel" in the city.Meza-Flores was subsequently taken to Mexico City, the defence ministry said.Baseball game interrupted as gunfire spreadsThe violence spilled into Guasave on Friday night, forcing the suspension of a baseball match at Kuroda Park.Fans watching the game between Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave rushed out of the stands as gunfire rang out.An video showed players fleeing the field midway through the match."It's being suspended… there's a situation happening off the field," CNN quoted the announcers telling the viewers. "We wish first and foremost to ask God that everything is OK… there is a national security incident, it may be better for us to go to break now."Who is Fausto Isidro Meza-FloresMeza-Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro", heads the Meza-Flores criminal organisation, or Los Mazatlecos, based in Guasave.He is listed among the FBI's 10 most-wanted fugitives. The agency had announced a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest.According to the FBI wanted poster, he is "allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States".He was indicted in 2019 on drug trafficking violations and possession of a firearm charges. He had also faced drug trafficking charges in 2012, the FBI poster said.The US Treasury Department said in a 2013 statement that the Meza-Flores cartel had been involved in "an extremely violent turf war" with the rival Sinaloa Cartel, which was then led by Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán. Guzmán is now serving a prison sentence in the US.Mexico's defence ministry said the operation to arrest Meza-Flores was conducted with US assistance.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
